title: Spiking Neural Networks
intro: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are networks of model neurons that talk to each other with discrete, time-stamped spikes. Time is part of the computation, not a side effect of it.

blocks.text: In a conventional artificial neural network, each unit outputs a real number, and a layer computes all of its outputs at once. In a spiking neural network, each neuron carries an internal state, its membrane potential, that evolves continuously in time. Input spikes arrive through synapses, each scaled by a synaptic weight, and nudge the membrane potential up or down. When the potential crosses a threshold the neuron emits a spike, an all-or-nothing event, and resets. Between spikes nothing is sent at all.

Three consequences follow. First, information can live in when spikes happen, not only in how many there are, so encoding becomes a design choice: rate coding, temporal coding, latency and population codes. Second, computation is sparse and event-driven: a silent neuron costs nothing to communicate, which is why neuromorphic hardware can run SNNs at very low power. Third, learning can use local timing: spike-timing-dependent plasticity changes a synapse from the relative timing of the spikes on either side of it, with no global error signal.

items: Neuron models: the rule that turns input current into spikes. Start with the leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, then see how adaptation, exponential spike initiation and ion channels add realism (#/snn/neuron-models).
Spike encoding: how a real-valued signal such as a pixel, a sound or a touch becomes spike trains (#/snn/encoding).
Neuron filters: how synapses and membranes smooth spike trains in time, which is what lets one neuron read another's output (#/snn/neuron-filters).
Learning rules: STDP and its variants, three-factor rules with eligibility traces, the BCM rule and surrogate gradients (#/snn/learning-rules).

blocks.text: How SNNs differ from the networks you may know

items: State: every neuron integrates over time, so an SNN is a dynamical system, not a stack of functions.
Communication: binary events with timing, instead of dense floating-point vectors.
Differentiability: a spike is a step function with zero derivative almost everywhere, so plain backpropagation fails; surrogate gradients or local rules take its place.
Hardware: SNNs map naturally onto event-driven chips (Loihi, TrueNorth, SpiNNaker) with memory placed beside compute.
Biology: SNNs are the natural language for models of real cortex, including cortical columns.

blocks.text: A suggested learning path toward cortical columns

The person who keeps this library wants to understand computational cortical columns and the Thousand Brains theory well enough to build a mini-brain from spiking neurons. The path below goes from single neurons to columns. Each step has an interactive simulation.

items: 1. One neuron: #/snn/neuron-models/lif, then #/snn/neuron-models/izhikevich and #/snn/neuron-models/adex for the firing patterns real cortical cells show.
2. Why neurons behave as they do: #/neuroscience/neuronal-dynamics (phase planes, excitability), with #/snn/neuron-models/fhn as the worked example.
3. Getting signals in and out: #/snn/encoding and #/snn/neuron-filters.
5. Dendrites as computers: #/snn/neuron-models/multicompartment. Prediction in HTM-style models lives on dendritic segments.
7. Putting it together: #/neuroscience/cortical-columns/column-blueprint, a practical plan for a spiking column.
8. Wider toolkits: #/foundations/nef (compiling functions into spiking populations), #/neuroscience/neural-manifolds, and #/neuromorphic-hardware for running it at scale.

blocks.text: Tip: highlight any technical term on a page, such as "membrane potential" or "eligibility trace", to see its definition inline and jump to the page that explains it.

Sources: Gerstner, Kistler, Naud & Paninski, Neuronal Dynamics: From Single Neurons to Networks and Models of Cognition (Cambridge University Press, 2014); Maass, "Networks of spiking neurons: the third generation of neural network models" (Neural Networks, 1997); Hawkins, Ahmad & Cui, "A Theory of How Columns in the Neocortex Enable Learning the Structure of the World" (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2017).
